sentences.html: Miguel is 11 years old and studies in Medellín. One ordinary day at a bus stop after school, a situation involving a message begins to change the plans for the afternoon.
Valentina is nearby and notices that Miguel is paying close attention to what is happening.
The first reaction seems simple, but the details matter because the problem is really about tone, context and verifying information.
“This is my choice, but that is our shared space,” the student says.
Nobody has a perfect answer at first, so the group uses the information they have and checks what is still uncertain.
The message has only five words.
Next time, Miguel will read the whole message twice.
Miguel says, “I am sorry, I misunderstood.”

sentences.html: The situation becomes harder when a short message is misunderstood. Miguel feels pressure to react quickly.
Instead of having all the facts, the students hear different versions of what happened.
Valentina suggests checking the information before blaming anyone or making a promise that cannot be kept.
The family asks, “Is it yours?” and checks before moving anything.
The moment feels personal, but it also connects with school life, family expectations, and the way young people communicate today.
Valentina reminds Miguel that asking for help can be a responsible decision when the situation is unclear.
Answering too fast can create problems.
One emoji changes the meaning of the message.
Miguel thinks the friend is angry, but that is not true.
A voice message would explain the tone better.

sentences.html: Miguel decides to take one small, concrete action in Medellín: ask clearly, verify a detail, protect someone’s privacy, or choose the safer option.
The action does not solve everything immediately, but it prevents the problem from growing.
Valentina explains that being responsible is not only about avoiding mistakes; it is also about correcting them when new information appears.
At home, they use technology every day, but they also set simple rules.
By the end of the day, the immediate problem has a result. Someone has to apologize, change a plan, return something, ask for help, or accept that the first idea was incomplete.
Miguel feels more confident because the decision came from evidence rather than pressure.
“What does this message mean?” Valentina asks.
Miguel waits before trying to reply.

sentences.html: At home, Miguel thinks about what could have happened if the group had reacted without checking anything.
